what: Kernel #1b block cost vs verify length, on a T4, real Inkling expert shapes

hardware.note: T4 has no FP8 datatype at all, so the E4M3 scales are decoded in software too, not just the FP4 codes

result.claim: Our batched dequant GEMM block cost is nearly flat in verify length.
result.evidence: w13 block cost goes 10.81 ms at N=1 to 6.44 ms at N=32, a 1.7x spread while the block gets 32x wider. From N=2 to N=8 it is flat at 5.29 to 5.35 ms. Per-token cost falls from 10.81 ms to 0.20 ms, a 54x drop.
result.contrast_with_strata: Strata block cost grew 62.7 ms to 940.5 ms over N=2..32, about 15x. Ours grows 1.2x over N=2..32. That is the gap the paper is about: one engine re-dequantises per token, ours dequantises once per block.

honest_caveats: Achieved bandwidth is only 2.9-6.4 GB/s against a 320 GB/s peak. The kernel is NOT yet bandwidth-efficient; it is flat because it is doing a small amount of work per block, not because it saturates memory. Optimisation headroom is large.
This measures the expert GEMM in isolation, not end-to-end decode. A full decode step also pays attention, routing and the loop passes.
w2 shows a sawtooth (2.5, 5.1, 2.7, 4.8, 3.5, 6.7 ms) rather than a clean curve. That is measurement noise from 30 iterations on a shared T4 and it is reported as seen, not smoothed.
Single run, one card, no repetition across sessions yet.
verdict: The precondition for speculative decoding paying on a T4 is met by our kernel and not by Strata's: verify cost does not scale with block size. Turning that into end-to-end tok/s needs the rest of the decode step and a bandwidth pass, and the 5-6 GB/s figure says there is real work left.
